problem: The sentence 'Exact universality with {H,T,CNOT} is false for every single-qubit rotation' is false. Many single-qubit rotations are exact members of the set — T itself is a rotation by π/8, and Z = T⁴, S = T², X = HZH are all exact finite products of H and T. The very next sentence of the chapter gives the correct claim (failure for angles that are not rational multiples of π), so the first sentence also contradicts it. A student will conclude that no rotation can ever be exact.
fix: Exact universality with {H,T,CNOT} is false: many single-qubit rotations cannot be written as a finite product of these gates. For example, a rotation by an angle that is not a rational multiple of π cannot be written as a finite product of H and T.

problem: 'a factor eiφ' is written as plain letters, not as e to the power iφ; read literally it looks like e × i × φ. The chapter's own style rule asks for Unicode superscripts, as used elsewhere (e<sup>iπ/4</sup>).
fix: If two circuits differ only by a factor e<sup>iφ</sup>, every measurement probability is unchanged.

problem: The lead defines a universal gate set as 'a small finite collection of gates', but Section 1 correctly allows continuous (infinite) sets such as arbitrary single-qubit rotations. The narrow definition can confuse a student who then meets continuous universal sets.
fix: A universal quantum gate set is a small collection of gates — often finite — from which any quantum circuit can be built.

problem: The intermediate powers are typed in LaTeX style, e^{iπ/2} and e^{iπ/4}, with braces, while the chapter otherwise uses Unicode superscripts (e<sup>iπ/4</sup>). Mixed notation looks untidy and braces read as literal characters on a phone.
fix: Write T² = diag(1, e<sup>iπ/2</sup>) = diag(1, i) and T = diag(1, e<sup>iπ/4</sup>), matching the earlier display.
